title: Should you listen to people who don't look like they lift?
summary: NH gives his 'trifecta' for whose fitness advice to trust: they currently demonstrate what they teach, have verifiable proof they did in the past, or have relevant credentials. Two disqualifiers override these: a record of lying or bad character, and lying about natural status. He trusts experience over theory but respects academics.

claims.claim: Whether to take advice from someone who doesn't look like they lift is almost a philosophical question: should you follow someone without outward signs of success?
NH partly agrees you don't need to be muscular or strong to understand how size and strength develop.
Rule 1: can the person demonstrate right now what they teach (big or strong now)?
Rule 2: if not, do they have tangible, verifiable proof (dated photos, official videos, recorded results) that they achieved it before, not just claims?
Rule 3: do they have credentials or diplomas in the field? Meeting any one of the three earns his ear; those with all three are the best to learn from.
NH meets only one criterion: he is young, has no sport-science diploma, and his body is his only proof.
Disqualifier 1: a demonstrated tendency to lie, hurt others or act cowardly undermines both their advice and their claimed feats; advice from someone you don't respect won't benefit you.
Disqualifier 2: natural status. He takes advice from openly enhanced people like John Meadows with a grain of salt, but lying about being natural is a deal breaker.
He is a bit colder toward academics who talk about building muscle but never did it, because he values experience over theory, though he deeply respects PhDs and science.
